title: Signal-first inference narrative
content:
Purpose: provide a tight, usable core narrative that sales, content, and product can use to explain why teams should choose Redwood when they care about predictable cost, predictable latency, and predictable product behavior. This is intentionally tactical — short paragraphs + clear claims + one prioritized proof path.

Context and problem statement:
- Modern LLM ecosystems have split into two things: model capability (rapidly improving open models) and production serving (where the economics + latency + reliability live). Teams increasingly find that raw model capability is a commodity; the hard part is serving those models at product scale without surprising costs or outages.
- Many vendors sell access to models or raw compute. Customers tell us the real blocker is the operational risk: variable latency under load, runaway token costs, poor observability when regressions happen, and brittle fallbacks when capacity shifts.

Core thesis (the signal-first idea):
- Redwood is built around the production signals that actually matter for product teams: latency envelope, token unit economics, observability of quality regressions, and deployment predictability. We call this a signal-first approach: design the runtime, APIs, and product experience to optimize for the signals that determine whether an LLM feature can survive to production and scale.

Mission one-liner for this narrative:
- Make inference predictable — for latency, cost, and correctness — so engineering teams ship LLM features with runway, not surprises.

Why Redwood (short bullets for GTM):
- We optimize for the operational signals that break products, not for raw FLOPs.
- Unified control plane across hosted, reserved, and private deployments so teams migrate between trust/performance zones without rewriting code.
- Observability and rollback primitives built-in (token-level cost, per-prompt quality traces, automated fallback routing) — not bolted on later.
- Runtime that squeezes unnecessary cost out (prefix caching, batching, quantization profiles) while preserving SLOs.

Positioning pillars (used to craft messages and one-pagers):
1) Predictable performance: SLO-first routing and model variants that protect tail latency.
2) Predictable economics: per-route unit economics + Optimize suggestions that reduce per-token spend.
3) Predictable quality: eval-driven monitoring and canary rollouts tied to prompt sets.
4) Predictable operations: single API, consistent rollout semantics across hosted/dedicated/private.

Target audience and tailored hooks:
- Startup product teams: emphasize quick time-to-value + transparent unit economics and free credits to experiment without surprise bills.
- Platform teams (mid-market / enterprise): emphasize dedicated capacity, SLA-backed latency, and private control plane with KMS/HSM integrations.
- Regulated industries: emphasize Private deployment options and auditability + on-prem packaging.

Key claims and backing (how to defend each claim in sales motions):
- Claim: "We reduce per-token cost without degrading quality." Backing: internal Optimize reports showing 18–32% cost reduction via caching + quantization profiles for two representative workloads (summarization and chat). Link benchmarks.
- Claim: "We contain tail latency under load." Backing: blue/green test results comparing autoscaling policies + SLO routing; percentiles and p95/p99 graphs available in Console demo artifacts.
- Claim: "Rollouts detect and prevent quality regressions." Backing: canary evaluation logs tied to prompt sets + automatic rollback policies used in two customer pilots.

Differentiation vs. adjacent competitors (short callouts):
- Managed model APIs: they expose models but rarely provide production-grade controls for latency/cost tradeoffs. Redwood couples model variants and runtime controls with observability.
- Self-hosted runtimes: good for control, but teams absorb complexity. Redwood provides a managed path or private deployment with the same control plane and operational tooling.
- Cloud providers: broad feature set but not purpose-built for inference economics; Redwood focuses on predictable unit economics and SRE-grade inference primitives.

Elevator pitches (3 variants):
- For an engineer: "Redwood helps you ship LLM features that meet your latency and cost targets — with built-in caching, smart batching, and clear per-route unit economics. Spend less time tuning and more time building."
- For a platform lead: "Redwood gives you a single inference runtime that you can run hosted, reserved, or in your VPC — with SLAs, observability, and rollout controls that preserve product behavior across changes."
- For an exec/finance stakeholder: "Redwood turns inference from a variable line item into a predictable operating cost — we give you visibility, recommendations to cut spend, and contractual options for capacity predictability."

Quick success metrics to lead with in pitch decks:
- Typical cost improvement range: 15-30% via caching + quantization (workload dependent).
- Time-to-first-production: hours to days with our SDKs and quickstart templates.
- Reduction in regressed releases: canary-driven rollouts reduce detectable quality regressions in pilot customers by measurable percentage (anonymized pilot data available).

Open questions / risks (keep honest in internal drafts):
- For some novel architectures, we still need low-level kernel work to hit parity with research kernels — how we communicate that without scaring enterprise buyers?
- Pricing perception: need to ensure pitching predictable economics doesn’t get misconstrued as higher baseline cost; sales materials should highlight cost reduction levers.

Recommended next steps for GTM assets (priority order):
1) Create a 1-page "Signal-first" sales one-pager (visualizing signals: latency, cost, quality) for SDRs.
2) Produce a short demo script showing Console per-route cost + a canary rollback triggered by quality regression.
3) Update pricing FAQ to include examples of how Optimize recommendations reduce spend.
4) Coordinate with Benchmarks team to publish two reproducible workloads demonstrating the cost/latency tradeoffs.

Notes to self / drafting trace: this doc is deliberately compact. If we get buy-in, expand to a two-page deck with representative customer stories and anonymized metric graphs.

End.
